boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Plymouth record (April 17-20, 1864) in Operations Against Plymouth [April-May 1864]. The interval covers the investment of Plymouth from the Washington road, the attacks on Fort Gray and the Eighty-fifth Redoubt, the Albemarle's descent on April 19 and the surrender on April 20; the May 5 action in Albemarle Sound is the separate record NC013 and is not added here. The live NPS campaign header 'Operations Against Plymouth and New Berne' and its April-May dates do not replace the frozen campaign or interval. Campaign-wide totals are context and are not assigned to one record. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field names the Plymouth garrison (4 infantry and artillery units) against Hoke's division; the frozen numeric bounds are blank and the live Forces Engaged field reads zero. Wessells's August 18 report, written from memory, gives the garrison 'at that time' as the Sixteenth Connecticut (400 effective men), Eighty-fifth New York (450), One hundred and first Pennsylvania (300) and One hundred and third Pennsylvania (400), a six-gun battery, a cavalry detachment, two heavy artillery companies and portions of two North Carolina companies; the four regimental figures sum to 1,550 (a computation). His April 17 dispatch relays citizens' report of five brigades; his report says the attackers, as subsequently ascertained, were Hoke's, Ransom's and Kemper's brigades with field batteries and cavalry. Cooke brought the ram Albemarle and says he had only 20 seamen from Charleston; he gives the Southfield six guns and a crew of 117 (read '1 17' in OCR) and the Miami 13 guns.
claims.rationale: Partial one-side figures with different bases: Wessells's effective men per regiment on about April 17 (reported four months later from memory), with no figure for artillery, cavalry or the North Carolina companies; unit identifications for the attackers; and ship armament and crew. The compiled casualty return (2,834 killed, wounded and missing) is an outcome record, not a strength figure. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; the live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Wessells says the line of defense ran '2£' miles (apparently two and a half; OCR) from Fort Gray, two miles above the town on the river bank and separated from the main line by Welch's Creek and its marsh, to the crossing of Coneby Creek below the town; the Eighty-fifth Redoubt was a small detached work in front of the right, and Fort Williams an inclosed work in the center. Cooke says the high stage of the water let the Albemarle pass over the obstructions, that he passed a battery at Warren Neck with a 200-pounder Parrott and another in the town, and that the river is only 200 yards wide there. NPS instead says the Confederates captured 'Fort Comfort'.
claims.rationale: Works and river described by two interested reports and a summary; no map verification. The works predate the attack; their effect is not scored, so the phase is left unresolved. NPS's Fort Comfort is not named in the inspected reports.

claims.value: Cooke says part of the Albemarle's machinery broke down on the night of the 17th and was repaired with a portable forge after about six hours, that the rudder-head then broke with a further four hours' delay, and that he moved the boat down stern foremost nearly all the way; after the surrender he reports immense quantities of commissary and other stores and probably 200 tons of anthracite coal captured. Wessells says the transport Massasoit carried women, children and non-combatants to Roanoke Island and that covered excavations along the line kept his loss comparatively slight.
claims.rationale: Readiness and material statements from interested reports; no supply or ammunition return was inspected. The capture of stores is post-outcome.

claims.value: Wessells says that on the 13th his information was positive enough to request 5,000 men, but that on the 16th, having learned that no considerable force was on the Roanoke, he let the Tacony return on the 17th, 'and this decision is to be regretted'; the ram's construction was too well watched for him to obtain positive information, and she passed down on the 19th unnoticed. Cooke says that, failing to hear from the army, he knew nothing of the enemy's batteries and obstructions until Gilbert Elliott reconnoitered them by boat, and that Elliott later reached Hoke by water and brought back dispatches.
claims.rationale: Retrospective statements by the two commanders about what they knew; the warning letters themselves were not selected.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Hoke (Major General) and Wessells (Colonel). Wessells's reports are headed and signed as Brigadier General, and Cooke calls Hoke Brigadier General; the frozen and live ranks are kept as recorded and not adopted. Wessells divided his line among Colonels Fardella, Lehmann and Beach, and Flusser directed the naval force; he says Colonel Mercer commanded the column at the Eighty-fifth Redoubt. Hoke requested the interview at which surrender was demanded, and Wessells hoisted the white flag 'in compliance with the earnest desire of every officer'. Cooke acted 'in obedience to your order' from the Navy Secretary and turned his prisoners over to Hoke.
claims.rationale: Roles attributed by the inspected reports. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit; subordinates who acted (Fardella, Lehmann, Beach, Flusser, Mercer, Cooke, Elliott) are named as attributed actors, not rated.

claims.value: The frozen result is a Confederate victory, and NPS says the garrison surrendered on the 20th. Wessells says he surrendered at 10 a.m. on April 20 with all the post contained, after the Confederates carried his left and captured Battery Worth; Cooke says the town was surrendered unconditionally at 12 m. that day. On the ram's action of the 19th, Cooke says he sank the Southfield and the Miami escaped after he struck her several times; Wessells says the Southfield was sunk and Flusser killed. NPS names the sunk vessel the 'Smithfield'.
claims.rationale: The outcome agrees; the surrender hour differs (10 a.m. against 12 m.) and the NPS vessel name differs from both reports. Kept as recorded. Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty field reads 2,834 total; the live page reads 3200 total (US 2900; CS 300). The compiled Union return printed as addenda to Wessells's report gives killed, wounded and missing of 127 officers and 2,707 men, 2,834 in all, by command. Wessells, unable to report losses, believed his own casualties did not exceed 150 and gives, from medical officers, the lowest Confederate killed and wounded as 850. Cooke reports one man killed on the Albemarle and eight prisoners picked up by his small boat.
claims.rationale: The frozen 2,834 equals the printed total of the compiled Union return (which includes the missing, that is the captured garrison); this is an observation, not a reconciliation, and the frozen figure's basis is not otherwise established. Wessells's 150 names no category. Confederate army losses are estimates relayed by Wessells; no Confederate return was inspected. The live figures are not adopted. Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: Butler's No. 1 dispatches and Peck's No. 2 reports (Volume XXXIII; read in part, not selected), Palmer's No. 5 report, the No. 6 record of events, Butts's No. 4 report, the naval reports of the Miami and Ceres (Official Records of the Navies, Volume 9), any Hoke or Confederate army report, and maps remain deferred. The Confederate Congress resolution, the Navy Secretary's extract and J. Taylor Wood's April 21 telegram were read in Volume 9 but not selected.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Wessells's dispatch and report (Official Records Series I, Volume XXXIII), Cooke's reports and Melancton Smith's reports (Official Records of the Navies, Series I, Volume 9) are separate families of interested participants' accounts; the volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. No 19th-century history was inspected for this campaign. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
